extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of poetry and literary style (aspiring poets and literary scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for judging and producing poetic style and diction, including what makes a poem 'essential', how diction should resist paraphrase, and pedagogical notes on forming taste and avoiding common faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability into simpler words is a defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is translatable in other and simpler words of the same language, without loss of sense or dignity, is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a maxim of criticism and reiterated: lines that can be rendered into plainer words without diminishing sense or feeling are 'vicious' in diction. (N.B. 'dignity' means absence of ludicrous and debasing associations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential poetry = works to which we most willingly return
rubrics_metrics.description: Not the poem which we have read, but that to which we return with the greatest pleasure, possesses the genuine power and claims the name of essential poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion privileges enduring, repeatable pleasure over transient novelty or single occasions of wonder; it is a test of a poem's genuine power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity of style = absence of ludicrous/debasing associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dignity in diction is defined as the absence of ludicrous and debasing associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a qualifier to the translatability maxim: preserving 'dignity' means avoiding language or images that produce ludicrous or degrading associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of stale similes, introductions, transitions, and petty self-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain introductions, similes, and examples were placed by name on a list of interdiction (e.g., the repeated example of 'Alexander and Clytus' was ultimately banished as overused).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives the example of an 'index expurgatorius' of well-known recurring phrases (including modest egoisms and flattering illeisms) that should be avoided; overused examples and habitual phrases become meaningless and should be purged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of sentence placement and structural coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences and clauses must be appropriate to the thesis under which they appear; teachers compared multiple exercises side-by-side and asked why a particular sentence could not fit under another thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no satisfactory answer could be returned, and two faults of the same kind were found in one exercise, the work was torn up and rewritten. This enforces precision of argument, cohesion, and correct placement of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid translating prose thoughts into poetical language (naturalness of diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The style characterised as 'translations of prose thoughts into the language of poetry' is criticised; genuine poetry uses natural language, not bookish or artificial phrase-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge and the author argue for metre and diction grounded in actual poetic feeling and native English usage rather than latinate, imitated, or mechanically 'fine' phrasing; beware school-taught artifices (e.g., Latin-verse habits) that produce prosaic thought dressed as verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration should be an everywhere-present under-current, not isolated exclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine admiration of a great poet is a continuous under-current of feeling; it is everywhere present, but seldom as a separate excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish true, sustained admiration from theatrical markers of admiration (e.g., ostentatious cleverness or repeated exclamatory emphasis at line-ends). Exclude from 'worthy feelings' the pleasure derived solely from novelty or the author's display of cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious cleverness and novelty for their own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure derived from mere novelty in the reader, and the desire to excite wonderment at the author's powers, are excluded from worthy feelings; French tragedies are mocked for 'two marks of admiration at the end of each line' as hieroglyphics of the author's self-admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of works that trade on dazzling cleverness or manufactured surprises rather than deep, continuous feeling; beware rhetorical devices that call attention to the author's own cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and unchangeability of great poets' diction
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be scarcely more difficult to alter a word or the position of a word in Milton or Shakespeare (in their most important works at least) without making the poet say something else, or something worse, than he does say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High poetic excellence shows itself in diction so exact that small alterations break the effect or meaning; value precision and fitness of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer passionate flow and genuine 'mother English' over intellectual subtleties or glittering imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Older (faulty) poets might have fantastic thoughts but in pure native English; moderns often present obvious thoughts in language of false beauty—glare, glitter, broken heterogeneous imagery, or an 'amphibious' mix of image and abstract meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic favours poetry where heart and passionate flow are preserved; warns against sacrificing feeling to intellect (older poets) or surrendering both to mere point and drapery (moderns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical balance: memory, models, and avoidance of premature disputatiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should, when memory predominates in youth, store facts for later judgment and awaken fond love and admiration by noble models; modes of teaching that make children prodigies of disputatiousness produce self-conceit, shallowness, arrogance, and infidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to teachers and curriculum designers: cultivate memory and taste first, use exemplary models to inspire admiration rather than training children chiefly to dispute and 'decide' prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on classical phraseology and mechanical borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: A custom of picking halves and quarters of lines from Virgil, Gradus, etc., to 'embody' thoughts leads to lyrics depending on authority rather than original thought; Latin-verse training can encourage dependence on adopted phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While classical learning has uses, beware that mechanical borrowing from classical models can produce translations of prose thoughts into verse and rob diction of native force and originality.
